title: Designing Pastebin

facts.text: A user enters text and gets a random link, then views the paste by its URL; pastes do not expire by default but may have a timed expiration; the service tracks monthly visits, deletes expired pastes and stays available.
Out of scope are registering an account, verifying email, logging in, editing the document, setting visibility and letting the user choose the shortlink.

Traffic is not evenly distributed, pastes are text only and analytics need not be realtime; assume 10 million paste writes and 100 million reads per month (10:1), which is 4 writes and 40 reads per second on average.
Each paste is about 1.27 KB (1 KB of content, 7-byte shortlink, 4-byte expiration, 5-byte created_at, 255-byte paste_path), which means 12.7 GB of new content per month and ~450 GB in 3 years.

A relational database can act as a large hash table mapping the generated url to a file server and path; instead of a file server, use a managed object store such as Amazon S3 or a NoSQL document store.
A NoSQL key-value store is an alternative to the relational hash table, and the answer should discuss the trade-offs between SQL and NoSQL.
In the pastes table, a primary key on the shortlink column creates an index that enforces uniqueness, and an extra index on created_at speeds lookups to log time instead of a full table scan.

To generate the unique url, take the MD5 hash of the user's ip_address plus timestamp (or of random data), Base 62 encode it and keep the first 7 characters: 62^7 values suffice for 360 million shortlinks in 3 years.

Base 62 encodes to [a-zA-Z0-9], which suits urls without escaping special characters, and is deterministic; Base 64 is another popular encoding but its additional + and / characters cause issues for urls.

To create a paste, the Web Server, a reverse proxy, forwards the request to the Write API server, which generates a unique url, regenerates on a duplicate, saves to the SQL pastes table and Object Store, and returns the url.

To view a paste, the Web Server forwards the request to the Read API server, which checks the SQL Database for the url, fetches the contents from the Object Store if found, and otherwise returns an error message.
Clients use a public REST API, and internal communications could use Remote Procedure Calls.
Because realtime analytics are not required, MapReduce the Web Server logs to get hit counts; the Analytics Database could be a data warehouse such as Amazon Redshift or Google BigQuery.
To delete expired pastes, scan the SQL Database for entries whose expiration timestamp is older than the current timestamp and delete them or mark them as expired.
Do not jump straight to the final design: state that scaling is iterative, benchmark and load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, and repeat.

An object store like S3 handles 12.7 GB of new content per month; a memory cache serves popular content for the 40 average reads per second and traffic spikes, and SQL read replicas handle the cache misses.

notes: The 4 paste writes per second fit on a single SQL write master-slave, otherwise federation, denormalization, SQL tuning or moving data to NoSQL (sents 2fa9ad8de136, 2960630d9eb1, e329c7154f31); cut for the 16-fact cap. The primer's conversion guide (seconds per month) is left to the estimation chapter.

definition.text: A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link.

facts.text: Each stored text entry is commonly called a paste, and account holders can typically edit or delete their pastes at any time.
Accounts let users manage and organize their content, and many platforms let users set a paste as public or private.
Pastebins may add features such as commenting, rendering markup like Markdown or ReStructuredText, or version control.
Pastebins arose for chatrooms, where sending large blocks of computer data disrupts closely interleaved conversation, so users are told to paste elsewhere and share the link.
Designing a pastebin is like designing a URL shortener, except that the service stores the paste contents instead of the original unshortened URL.
